asset_supply_slow(k1).text: The supply of the affected firms' assets is fixed or slowly expandable.

beneficiaries_organize(k1).text: The protected producers can organize to influence renewal at a cost below their stake.

binding(k1).text: The domestic price rises by a substantial part of the tariff; foreign sellers do not absorb most of it.

can_relocate_capital(k1).text: Some downstream users can move production abroad when they replace plant.

competitors_exempt(k1).text: Many downstream users compete with sellers who do not face the higher input cost.

domestic_substitutes(k1).text: Domestic producers make close substitutes for the covered imports.

enforcement_budget_raised(k1).text: The administering agency's budget is raised to cover the new work, so taxpayers fund it.

expected_to_last(k1).text: Investors expect the measure to stay in force for at least its stated term.

expects_extension(k1).text: The protected producers expect the measure to be renewed or extended.

exporters_price_takers(k1).text: The exporting users sell at world prices and cannot pass the higher cost on.

harmed_organize(k1).text: The harmed users can organize to seek repeal or exemption at a cost below their stake.

input_not_replaceable(k1).text: The taxed good is a material part of downstream costs and cannot be replaced at the old cost.

no_offset(k1).text: Lower imports reduce foreigners' purchases of the country's exports in the medium run; capital flows do not cancel it.

relief_discretionary(k1).text: Relief is granted case by case at officials' discretion.

relief_valuable(k1).text: Relief is worth more to applicants than its fee.

reshaping_pays(k1).text: Reshaping goods to fall outside the definitions costs some actors less than the burden.

substitute_supply_expands(k1).text: Sellers of the uncovered substitutes can expand their supply.

evidence: Halvern buys a small share of the world's steel.
answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-1 (binding): imports remain a meaningful share of supply and foreign sellers do not absorb most of the tariff; Halvern buys a small share of world steel.

question.text: Will the price domestic buyers pay for the covered goods rise by a substantial part of the tariff, rather than foreign sellers absorbing most of it?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-2 (substitutability): domestic mills can raise output from spare or idle capacity and produce close substitutes for most imports.

question.text: Do domestic producers make goods that buyers can use in place of the covered imports, so that dearer imports send buyers to them?

evidence: Halvern is a mid-sized trading country with its own currency and a floating exchange rate.
answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-8: the fall in steel imports is not offset by capital flows or other adjustments within the medium horizon.

question.text: When the country buys fewer imports, foreigners earn less of its currency. Through the exchange rate (the currency rises against what it would otherwise be) this makes the country's exports dearer abroad, so export industries sell less: that is the mechanism, not an offset to it. Over the medium run, will this chain operate, rather than being cancelled by foreigners investing or lending more in the country?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-14 (substitutability): steel is a material part of construction costs and builders cannot replace it at the old cost in the medium run. Applied to both downstream groups.

question.text: Will the downstream users' costs rise materially because of the higher price of the taxed good (given how much of it they use and whether they can switch to other materials or designs in the medium run)?

evidence: Imported fabricated steel products and finished goods containing steel (machinery, vehicles, appliances, fabricated structural sections, fasteners) are not covered.
answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-7 (substitutability): many steel users compete with imported finished goods that are not taxed.

question.text: Do the downstream users compete with sellers who do not face the higher cost (imported finished goods, untaxed products)?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-16 (revenue_use): the budgets of customs and the exclusion office are raised to cover the new work.

question.text: Will the budget of the agency that administers the measure be raised to cover the new work, rather than the work being absorbed within its existing budget?

evidence: Imported fabricated steel products and finished goods containing steel are not covered.
answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-3: some imports can be reshaped to fall outside the tariff's definitions at a cost below 25%.

question.text: For some of the actors bound by the measure, will reshaping goods so that they fall outside the measure's definitions cost less than the measure would cost them?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-5: exclusions are decided case by case, with weight given to objections from the mills.

question.text: Will the officials who grant exclusions, waivers or exemptions decide case by case, with room to weigh who the applicant is or what others say against it, rather than by a fixed published test?

evidence: Exclusions last one year and must be renewed.
answer.rationale: No row of WE-013's assumption table covers this premise on its own; the probability is an illustrative figure chosen for this fixture, not a table value. WE-013 treats an exclusion as valuable (C-11 text), but A-5 covers only the discretion.

question.text: Is an exclusion, waiver or exemption worth more to those who apply than the fee for applying?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-6: steelmakers and users organize to influence renewal and exclusions. A-6 joins both groups; the same figure is used for each of the two questions.

question.text: Can the protected domestic producers organize to influence the renewal or extension decision at a cost lower than what they stand to gain?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-6: steelmakers and users organize to influence renewal and exclusions. A-6 joins both groups; the same figure is used for each of the two questions.

question.text: Can the downstream users who cannot pass the higher cost on organize to seek repeal, exemption or non-renewal at a cost lower than what they stand to lose?

evidence: A review in the third year may extend it.
answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-10 (expectations): steelmakers expect the tariff to be renewed at the year-three review.

question.text: Do the protected domestic producers expect the measure to be renewed or extended when it comes up for review?

evidence: Importers of record must pay a tariff of 25% of the customs value on imports of flat-rolled and long steel products, for three years.
answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-11 (expectations): investors expect the tariff to stay in force for at least its three-year term.

question.text: Do investors expect the measure to stay in force for at least its stated term?

answer.rationale: No row of WE-013's assumption table covers this premise on its own; the probability is an illustrative figure chosen for this fixture, not a table value. SB-4 needs assets in fixed or slowly expandable supply; WE-013 leaves it implicit for mills and plants with specific capital.

question.text: Is the supply of the affected firms' productive assets (plants, equipment, the shares that claim their returns) slow to expand or to replace?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-9 (mobility): some steel-using firms have the option of producing abroad when plants are replaced.

question.text: Do some downstream users have the option of producing abroad when they next replace their plants?

evidence: Imported fabricated steel products and finished goods containing steel are not covered.
answer.rationale: No row of WE-013's assumption table covers this premise on its own; the probability is an illustrative figure chosen for this fixture, not a table value. RS-1 needs the substitute's supply to be able to expand for quantity_substitute to rise as a traded quantity; WE-013 leaves it implicit (A-7 covers competition only).

question.text: Can the sellers of the uncovered substitutes (imported finished goods) supply more at roughly their present prices?

evidence: machinery makers export about 35% of their output
answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-013 (illustrative figures), A-15 (substitutability): Halvern's machinery exporters sell at prices set in world markets.

question.text: Do the downstream users who export sell at prices set in world markets, so that they cannot pass a higher input cost on to foreign buyers?

components.cap_unit: ad valorem, share of customs value, for three years
source_sentences: Importers of record must pay a tariff of 25% of the customs value on imports of flat-rolled and long steel products, for three years.
Imported fabricated steel products and finished goods containing steel (machinery, vehicles, appliances, fabricated structural sections, fasteners) are not covered.
A review in the third year may extend it.
Steel users may apply to exclude a product "not produced domestically in sufficient quantity or quality".

context: Three domestic steel firms supply about 60% of the steel used in Halvern; the rest is imported (WE-013 record).
About 4,000 domestic manufacturers use steel as a main input; machinery makers export about 35% of their output (WE-013 record).
The mills buy scrap, ore and energy as inputs, and their shares are held by owners (WE-013 table, C-21 and C-23; not stated in the order's text).
Halvern buys a small share of the world's steel and has a floating exchange rate (WE-013 record).
